With-skill is perfectly consistent (0% stddev on pass rate) vs. 11% stddev on baseline — the skill removes the variance, not just the misses.

Without-skill failures cluster on operational gotchas that aren't load-bearing in any single doc page: eval-2 baseline used inline import for a 50k-doc hourly job (no FULL reconciliation possible), didn't set acl_enabled=True at datastore creation, and left ACL strategy as an open item. These are the kinds of bugs that only surface in production.

Eval-0 baseline chose Snowflake-managed MCP server + Cortex Analyst — arguably a stronger architecture than the with-skill answer in some shops, but it cost it three assertions that assumed Cloud Run hosting. The 'cloud_run_deployment' assertion may be over-specified; consider broadening to 'managed HTTPS hosting'.

Baseline does well on widely-documented patterns (StreamableHTTP transport, the exact OAuth redirect URI) — these are findable with web search. Skill outperforms on combinations of patterns and the specific failure modes (IMS prefix asymmetry, acl_enabled-at-creation immutability, LIMIT injection in run_query).

Time is 13% faster with skill (222s vs 257s) and far less variable (31s stddev vs 99s stddev). Token usage is slightly higher with skill (+10%) — the skill is making the agent do more rigorous scaffolding, not skipping work.

Several with-skill graders flagged eval-design concerns: assertions that check for topic mentions rather than verifying the code does the right thing. Worth tightening in iteration 2 if we run one — e.g., 'GCS JSONL not inline' could verify GcsSource is actually called in code, not just that JSONL is mentioned in prose.
